## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a12-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- a12-explain:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Same lever, different hands</dt><dd>At the defaults each instrument cuts 34% to 38% of CO₂ for $22 to $23 per t avoided; the money that changes hands runs from $39.4M to $136.0M a year.</dd>
<dt>Per tonne avoided</dt><dd>The change in resource cost ÷ the CO₂ avoided, both against no policy: at $30 per t, $41.6M ÷ 1.83 Mt = $23 per t. Carbon payments are left out.</dd>
<dt>Carbon price</dt><dd>Raises every gas MWh's cost; gas plants pay $88.5M a year at $30 per t.</dd>
<dt>Credits</dt><dd>Lower the cost of new wind and solar; taxpayers pay. A $30 production credit costs $46 per t avoided, against $23 per t at $10.</dd>
<dt>Investment credit</dt><dd>Paid up front: $681.3M at 30%, or $39.4M a year spread over the plants' life at 4%.</dd>
<dt>Standard</dt><dd>Requires a clean share. If certificates trade at the marginal compliance cost, $9.39 per MWh at 65%, customers would spend $136.0M a year, wind that ran anyway included.</dd>
<dt>Real costs and transfers</dt><dd>The resource cost changes only with the plan; payments between groups are transfers.</dd>
</dl>
<!-- a12-explain:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Real costs and transfers</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Resource cost.** What the plan uses up: new plants' capital and fixed upkeep, and the gas plants' fuel and variable upkeep. It changes only when the plan changes.
- **Transfers.** Carbon payments, credits and certificate payments move money between groups; they add up to zero across society, so they are left out of the resource cost.
- **Who bears them in the end** depends on prices and contracts: a carbon payment can reach customers' bills, a credit can lower them. This model does not trace that.
- **Equal cuts.** Compare cost per tonne avoided between instruments only at similar cuts: the cost of the next tonne rises as the cut deepens.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Each instrument as an edit of one LP</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Carbon price** $\tau$ (\$ per t): each gas MWh's cost $c_g$ (\$ per MWh) becomes $c_g + \tau\, e_g$, with $e_g$ its CO₂ in t per MWh.
- **Production credit** $\pi$ (\$ per MWh): each new wind and solar MWh used costs $-\pi$.
- **Investment credit** $\iota$ (a share): each new plant's annual capital cost is multiplied by $1 - \iota$.
- **Clean-energy standard** $s$ (a share): one more rule, $\sum_t w_t\, \mathit{clean}_t \ge s \sum_t w_t\, d_t$. Its dual, a [shadow price]{.lx-term term="shadow-price"}, is the cost of one more required MWh.
- **Symbols.** $t$: an hour of the six days; $w_t$: the days it stands for; $\mathit{clean}_t$: wind and sun used and $d_t$: demand, in MW over one hour, so MWh.
- **Next.** [M6](m06-carbon-in-models.html) writes this LP out, caps CO₂ instead of pricing it, and adds a procurement rule.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Demand that answers to prices: here demand is the same under every instrument.</li>
<li>How the government raises or spends the money, and the instruments' interactions when several apply at once.</li>
<li>Timing: the plan is built at once, with perfect foresight of the six days.</li>
<li>Lines inside the grid, imports and exports, and the reliability value of new plants.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<!-- a12-check:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a12-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="same-cut" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Here, instruments that cut about the same CO₂ cost society about the same; they differ most in who pays.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact, in this model. The defaults cut 34% to 38% for $22 to $23 per t avoided, while the money that changes hands runs from $39.4M to $136.0M.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bigger-credit" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A bigger production credit buys each tonne as cheaply as a small one.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At $10 per MWh the plan avoids CO₂ at $23 per t; at $30, at $46 per t, with 1.7 TWh of wind and sun curtailed.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="standard-free" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A clean-energy standard costs nothing, because it costs taxpayers nothing.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At 65% the resource cost rises by $36.3M a year. If customers fund certificates at the marginal compliance cost, they spend $136.0M.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="battery" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Any policy that favors clean power gets batteries built.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth, here</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, here. No slider setting builds a battery: under these costs and six representative days, its energy-shifting savings do not cover its annual cost. Reserves and other reliability services are not valued.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a12">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="price" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A combined-cycle plant emits 0.40 t of CO₂ per MWh. By how much does a $30 carbon price raise its cost per MWh?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$12.00</li><li data-value="b">$30.00</li><li data-value="c">$75.00</li><li data-value="d">$0.40</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$12.00: $30 per t × 0.40 t per MWh. $30 forgets the rate; $75 divides by it.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<!-- a12-check:end -->
```

## Numbers, sources and what's next
:::

::: {.lx-end}
```{=html}
<!-- a12-rules:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world: one rule of each kind</p>
<ul class="a12-rules">
<li><p><b>Carbon price · European Union.</b> EU Emissions Trading System.</p><p>A cap-and-trade scheme, launched in 2005: a cap limits total emissions, and covered plants, electricity and heat generation among them, surrender one allowance, a permit to emit, per tonne of <span class="lx-term" data-term="co2e">CO₂ equivalent</span>.</p><p class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://climate.ec.europa.eu/eu-action/carbon-markets/about-eu-ets_en">European Commission, About the EU Emissions Trading System (page updated 13 May 2026)</a>, read 5 November 2026.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Production credit · United States, federal.</b> Clean electricity production credit, tax code section 45Y.</p><p>For wind and solar, Public Law 119-21 (2025) ends it for plants that begin construction after 4 July 2026 and enter service after 31 December 2027.</p><p class="lx-hint">Source: IRS, Notice 2025-42, Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-36, sections 1 and 2.02, 2 September 2025; read 5 November 2026.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Investment credit · United States, federal.</b> Clean electricity investment credit, tax code section 48E.</p><p>The same law sets the same end dates for wind and solar plants.</p><p class="lx-hint">Source: IRS, Notice 2025-42, Internal Revenue Bulletin 2025-36, sections 1 and 2.02, 2 September 2025; read 5 November 2026.</p></li>
<li><p><b>Clean-energy standard · California.</b> Renewables Portfolio Standard (a renewables-only standard).</p><p>Senate Bill 100 (2018) raised it to 60% of retail electricity sales by 2030, from eligible renewable plants, such as wind and solar, anywhere in the Western Electricity Coordinating Council's region.</p><p class="lx-hint">Source: California Public Utilities Commission, Renewables Portfolio Standard (RPS) Program page, read 5 November 2026.</p><p>For scale: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory counted 16 states that had adopted a 100% clean electricity standard, with data through 2023.</p><p class="lx-hint">Source: <a href="https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/publications/us-state-renewables-portfolio-clean-0">Barbose, U.S. State Renewables Portfolio &amp; Clean Electricity Standards: 2024 Status Update, LBNL (August 2024)</a>, read 5 November 2026.</p></li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-hint">The model's instruments are simpler than these rules: no phase-outs, eligibility tests or trading.</p>
</div>
<!-- a12-rules:end -->
```

```{=html}
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_08_02.html">Electric Power Annual, Table 8.2</a> and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_07_04.html">Table 7.4</a>, 2025 data; <a href="https://www.eia.gov/environment/emissions/co2_vol_mass.php">Carbon Dioxide Emissions Coefficients</a>.</li>
<li>Earlier lessons: <a href="a01-project-tea.html">A1</a> (a project's cash flows), <a href="12-trade-offs.html">lesson 12</a> (a carbon price on a plan), <a href="08-merit-order.html">lesson 8</a> (production credits and negative prices), <a href="a10-emissions-questions.html">A10</a> (the Plains Grid).</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
